• Initiative: SEBI introduced the Credit Risk-

• Coverage: Listed and proposed-to-be-
listed non-convertible securities, commercial 
papers, securitised debt instruments, 

 
  
  
  
  
 security receipts, and structured 
debt/market-linked debentures. 

• Six Credit Risk Levels: Existing credit 
ratings from AAA to D will be mapped to 
six colour-coded risk levels. 

- AAA: Lowest credit risk. 

- D: Highest risk category, associated with 
default. 

  • Key Rules: 

- Mandatory Disclosure: The Credit Risk-o-
Meter must be disclosed in offer documents, 
prospectuses, private placement 
memorandums, advertisements, and Online 
Bond Platform Providers’ (OBPPs) websites 
and mobile applications. 

- Multiple Credit Ratings: The meter will 
reflect the lowest rating when a security has 
ratings from multiple Credit Rating Agencies 
(CRAs). 

- Unsecured Debt: The word 
“UNSECURED” must appear in bold red 
text. 

- Rating Updates: OBPPs must update the 
meter within 24 hours of receiving rating-
change information from the National 
Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) or 
Central Depository Services (India) Limited 
(CDSL). 

- Manual Overrides: Prohibited; platforms 
must maintain audit trails.

International Affairs.question: upgraded from ‘BBB+’ to ‘A−’, marking the   country’s first rating upgrade in 2026. Which   credit rating agency upgraded India’s   sovereign rating?
International Affairs.explanation:
Answer: D 

• Agency: Japan Credit Rating Agency 
(JCR). 

The report titled Limiting Overshoot: 
Navigating Exceedance of 1.5°C and 
Pathways Towards Return highlighted 
the growing challenge of temporarily 
exceeding the 1.5°C global warming 
threshold and the need for rapid 
emissions reductions. Which 
organisation released this report? 

A.World Meteorological Organization 
(WMO) 

B.Intergovernmental Panel on Climate 
Change (IPCC) 

C.United Nations Development Programme 
(UNDP) 

D.United Nations Environment Programme 
(UNEP) 

E.International Energy Agency (IEA) 

• Rating Upgrade: India’s sovereign rating 

was upgraded from ‘BBB+’ to ‘A−’ in 2026. 

Explanation 

Answer: D 

• Significance: This was India’s first 
sovereign rating upgrade in 2026 and, 
according to the supplied information, the 
highest rating given to India by any rating 
agency. 

• Meaning of A−: Indicates a high level of 

certainty in honouring financial obligations. 

• Quick Recall: 

- JCR: Upgraded India from BBB+ to A−. 

• Report: Limiting Overshoot: Navigating 
Exceedance of 1.5°C and Pathways 
Towards Return. 

• Released By: United Nations 
Environment Programme (UNEP). 

• Core Message: Temporarily exceeding the 
1.5°C global warming limit is increasingly 
difficult to avoid in the near term. 

• Key Findings: 

 
  
  
  
 - 1.5°C Threshold: Human-induced warming 
has reached about 1.4°C above pre-
industrial levels and is increasing at around 
0.25°C per decade. 

- Probability of Exceedance: There is a 75% 
probability that the five-year mean 
temperature will exceed 1.5°C during 2026–
2030. 

- Remaining Carbon Budget: About 130 
billion tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO₂) 
remain for a 50% chance of staying within 
1.5°C from 2026. 

- Budget Exhaustion: At current emissions 
of roughly 40 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year, 
the remaining budget could be exhausted in 
about three years. 

- Cost of Delay: Every additional five years 
of sustained high emissions could add 
around 0.1°C to peak warming. 

- Impact of Past Emissions: Emissions since 
2015 have already increased the minimum 
achievable peak warming by about 0.2°C. 

- Current Policies: Projected median 
warming could reach around 2.6°C by 2100. 

- NDCs and Net-Zero Targets: Even if all 
current Nationally Determined Contributions 
(NDCs) and long-term net-zero targets are 
fully implemented, peak warming could still 
reach around 1.8°C.
